Module 2 · Underwriting

Which policy would approve it?

The simulator assigns this borrower a 7.9007% modeled probability of default using the application inputs and the model’s assumptions. Compare the two recorded decisions to see how each policy’s cutoff treated the same borrower.

Where did the 7.9007% come from?

Module 1 drew the near-prime band, generated a score of 654 within it and used the band’s starting default probability of 6%. It also generated the borrower’s credit utilization (57.88%) and debt-to-income ratio (32.81%). Utilization multiplied the estimate by 1.25. The DTI multiplier was 1.00. Three recent inquiries and five credit accounts each contributed a factor of 1.05. The requested payment used $322.14 ÷ $10,102.29 = 3.19% of monthly income. That payment-to-income ratio contributed a factor of 0.95, and the requested amount relative to income contributed 1.03. The remaining profile multipliers were 1. A repeatable adjustment for this application was 0.976486.

6% × 1.25 × 1.05 × 1.05 × 0.95 × 1.03 × 0.976486 ≈ 7.9007%. This case stayed in the model’s normal range. These multipliers are assumptions in a synthetic model. Estimating real default probabilities would require observed repayment outcomes.

Manual review. The baseline cutoff was 8%. The shaded borderline range ran from 7.60% to 8.40%. This application fell inside it.

What would approval add to the portfolio?

For a baseline auto loan, the simulator assumes the lender loses $45 of every $100 outstanding if the borrower defaults. That 45% is the loss given default (LGD). Weight it by the chance of default to estimate the loss on the offer.

$12,839.56 × 7.9007% × 45% = $456.49
Amount exposed × probability of default × loss given default

Baseline leaves the file in review. Growth adds one offer, $12,839.56 of offered credit and $456.49 of modeled loss. Customer take-up and repayment would determine the realized result.

This borrower was one of 2,839 applicants who gained an offer under Growth. All 1,476 who lost an offer had a Baseline counteroffer and moved to manual review under Growth. That left 1,363 additional offers across the same 50,000 requests. Inspect the Growth comparison (CG02).

Another auto applicant requested $66,131.71. Baseline offered $65,000. Growth left the request open for review. Trace the $65,000 counteroffer.

Why 45%, and when does it change?

Module 1 sets a loss rate for each product. The model assumes a lender can recover more from a secured mortgage than from an unsecured personal loan. These are adjustable assumptions. Calibrating them for a real portfolio would require observed defaults and recoveries.

Share of the outstanding balance lost if the borrower defaults
ProductBaselineBroad severity stress
Mortgage20%28%
Home equity line25%35%
Auto loan45%55%
Unsecured personal loan70%85%
Revolving line85%95%

In the secured and broad stress runs, this applicant still requested $12,839.56 and had a 7.9007% modeled default probability. Raising auto LGD to 55% lifted expected loss on the full request from $456.49 to $557.93. The stressed decisions went to manual review, so the engine recorded no offered amount.

How did the simulator build this borrower?

Module 1 · Synthetic applications

Where did this borrower come from?

Start with application APP-00032476. To build its credit profile, the SQL combines the application ID, a population ID and 15 numbered labels to produce 15 repeatable numbers between zero and one. The engine can reproduce each draw and reuse it in more than one calculation. Using the same IDs reproduces the draws, so a second policy can evaluate the same application.

  1. Assign a product and a credit score. One draw selects a product using the portfolio mix. Another selects a credit-score band. A third places the borrower within that band. This application becomes an auto loan with a near-prime score of 654.
  2. Build a financial profile. Each score band has an income range and a distribution. Applicants in the same band can earn different incomes, and neighboring bands can overlap. This applicant’s simulated annual income is $121,227.52. The engine also generates features such as debt burden, credit use and recent inquiries.
  3. Calculate affordability. For this $12,839.56 request, 48 monthly installments at a modeled 9.4304% annual rate give a $322.14 monthly payment. Divide by monthly income of $10,102.29 to get 3.19%. That is the share of gross monthly income this new payment would consume.
Reproduce the product and score assignments

Baseline assigns the first 30% of the product draw range to mortgages, the next 25% to revolving lines and the next 20% to auto loans. This application’s draw is 0.743735, inside the auto interval from 0.55 up to 0.75. Its separate score-band draw is 0.698823, inside the near-prime interval from 0.46 up to 0.70. For the 60 integer scores from 640 through 699, the score calculation is 640 + floor(60 × 0.241315) = 654. The draws shown here are rounded to six decimal places.

Baseline product and score mix · Repeatable draws · Assignment formulas

Why freeze the inputs? Keeping the population ID fixes the draws. Changing an assumption such as the product mix or interest rate can still change the generated application. To measure a policy change alone, both Module 2 policies read the same saved Module 1 scenario and population. The resulting comparison describes how the rules behave on these synthetic applicants. Its relevance to a particular bank depends on how closely the assumptions resemble that bank’s applicants.

Portfolio analytics

What changes across 50,000 applications?

Baseline is the reference policy. The challenger evaluates the same 50,000 applications with different rules. Choose a comparison to see who gained or lost an offer and how those offers changed the portfolio’s modeled loss.

Who gained or lost an offer?

All 1,476 lost offers were Baseline counteroffers that moved to manual review under Growth. These applications remained unresolved. Growth recorded a borderline profile as the primary reason for 1,021 and a debt-to-income review for 455.

For the $66,131.71 auto request, Growth raised the product limit from $65,000 to $71,500. The request now fit the limit, while the applicant’s 43.80% debt-to-income ratio met Growth’s borderline rule for its 46% approval threshold (43.70%–48.30%). Inspect the auto applicant’s two decisions.

Which decisions count as a gain or loss?

A gain moves an applicant from review or decline under baseline to an approval or counteroffer under the challenger. A loss is the reverse.

Findings and insights

Offer counts rose in both scenarios. Total credit offered moved in opposite directions.

Standard requests CG18
589 more offers, $187.54M less credit
Larger requests CG20
5,651 more offers, $62.23M more credit

Each policy evaluated the same 50,000 requests within its comparison. CG18 used the standard amounts. In CG20, 41,971 of those applicants requested more. The challenger widened entry to counteroffer testing and tightened offer sizing.

Which counteroffer rules changed?

More applicants with severe requested terms could qualify for a counteroffer test. For home equity lines, the maximum offer fell from $175,000 to $150,000, the target payment-to-income ratio from 22% to 20%, and the maximum modeled loss on an offer from $7,000 to $5,600. These comparisons measure the combined effects.

Standard requests CG18

The 29,014 applicants who had offers under both policies received $252.80 million less in total. That reduction outweighed the dollars added by new offers, even before counting lost offers. The average offer fell from $128,596 to $119,922.

One mortgage applicant received $655,000 under baseline and $615,000 under the challenger. Both policies made a counteroffer. That single borrower explains $40,000 of the reduction in the third row.

Larger requests CG20

The 6,347 applicants who gained an offer added $455.67 million. That exceeded the dollars removed from lost offers and from applicants offered credit under both policies. The average offer fell from $158,029 to $130,154, yet total credit offered rose.

One applicant requested a $312,500 home equity line. Baseline sent it to review. The challenger offered $150,000, adding one offer to the first row and $607.61 of modeled expected loss.

What else changed across the campaign?

Where did the applicants go when the review queue shrank?2,219 moved from manual review to decline. All 29,762 offers stayed in place.

CG06 changed the rule for handling a smaller offer that fails the lender’s tests. Baseline referred those cases to a person. The challenger declined them. Of 50,000 applicants, those 2,219 were the only ones whose decision changed. Reviews fell from 7,535 to 5,316, with identical dollars offered and identical modeled loss.

Follow the $43,880.83 personal loan through both policies to see where that rule took effect. An operational pilot could track whether human reviewers would have found a workable offer in any of the declined cases.

Compare the two review policiesInspect the personal loan

Why did a rate shock leave most default estimates unchanged?46,633 of 50,000 estimates held steady. The other 3,367 rose.

In the generator’s two-percentage-point rate shock, a payment could rise while staying in the same payment-to-income band. The model raises its risk multiplier when the payment crosses a band boundary.

Home equity application APP-00047266 crossed the 20% boundary. On this $250,000 interest-only line, the rate went from 12.8269% to 14.8269%. The rate increase added $250,000 × 2% ÷ 12 = $416.67 a month. The payment went from 18.84% to 21.78% of income, the multiplier rose from 1.25 to 1.45, and modeled default probability went from 22.85% to 26.51%.

Inspect the home equity line’s inputsCheck all 50,000 estimates

Which borrowers account for the most loss dollars?Near-prime mortgages accounted for one-third of baseline modeled loss on offers.

Under baseline policy M2-01, 2,752 near-prime mortgage offers totaled $706.36 million. At 2.75 cents of modeled loss per dollar offered, that added up to $19.40 million of the portfolio’s $58.55 million.

Deep-subprime revolving credit lines had the highest loss per dollar among the 25 product and credit-score groups at 29.70 cents. That rate came from a single $6,000 counteroffer, contributing $1,782 of modeled loss. The rate measures risk per dollar. The offer count and total dollars show how much of the portfolio it affects.

Compare baseline offers and losses by product and score

How can expected loss rise when the lender offers less credit?Under stressed recoveries, offers fell by $245.12 million and modeled loss rose by $6.90 million.

Runs M2-31 and M2-32 held the baseline lending policy and each applicant’s modeled default probability fixed. The stress scenario assumed the lender recovers less when a secured borrower defaults. Across the same 50,000 applicants, offers fell from 29,762 to 29,197, while expected loss on those offers rose from $58.55 million to $65.45 million.

For mortgage application APP-00000053, the request was $278,694.49 and the model estimated a 34.3171% chance of default. Raising the share lost in default from 20% to 28% increased expected loss on the request from $19,127.97 to $26,779.16. The baseline run offered $145,000. Under stressed recoveries, the counteroffer failed and the request went to manual review.

Inspect the saved totals for M2-31 and M2-32

Which questions would you take to a pilot?

Who takes the offer? Measure how often applicants accept a smaller amount, by product and risk band. The campaign counts offers. Acceptance and funding determine which offers become outstanding balances.

Does the expected loss match experience? Follow funded accounts over a common observation window. Allow time for defaults and recoveries to emerge, then compare realized losses with the model’s estimates.

Is the policy worth operating? Compare interest and fee income with funding costs, credit losses and servicing costs. Track the number of applications sent to review and the time each decision takes.

Code design flowcharts

Follow the data through either program. The archive written by Module 1 supplies the application records that Module 2 evaluates.

Module 1 · From synthetic application to expected loss

  1. Generate the applicant and the request

    The population ID fixes the random draws for each application ID. The scenario settings turn those draws into a product, score band, income, credit history, requested amount and terms.

  2. Price the request and calculate the monthly payment

    The product, borrower risk and rate environment shape the annual rate. The product determines which payment formula runs.

    • Mortgage, auto or personal loanSpread principal and interest over the loan term.
    • Revolving credit lineApply the minimum payment percentage plus a share of monthly interest.
    • Home equity lineEstimate an interest-only payment on the requested amount.

  3. Translate payment into default risk

    Divide monthly payment by gross monthly income. The resulting payment-to-income band modifies the score-based default estimate alongside borrower and product factors.

  4. Calculate loss and save the application

    Requested amount × modeled default probability × product loss given default. The saved scenario row gives Module 2 the original request, its affordability and its modeled loss before any policy decision.

Original design flow · BRD §5.1, pp. 9–10Payment branches in SQLLoss calculation in SQL

Module 2 · From a credit request to a policy decision

  1. Match the inputs to a policy

    The run selector identifies a Module 1 scenario, a lending strategy and product rules. Preflight checks verify that the inputs and settings agree before the decision rules run.

  2. Evaluate the rules in priority order

    Policy stops and severe risk or debt-to-income triggers take precedence. The next tests identify counteroffer candidates, cases requiring review and requests eligible for approval. A case that clears none of these tests goes to review.

  3. Resolve the decision

    • ApproveOffer the requested amount and carry forward its modeled loss.
    • Test a counterofferSize and round a smaller offer. Check its minimum size, maximum reduction, product cap, payment burden and loss limit. A pass yields a counteroffer. A failure goes to review or decline according to policy.
    • Manual reviewLeave the amount and loss unresolved pending a decision.
    • DeclineRecord zero offered dollars and zero modeled loss on the offer.

  4. Explain, archive and compare

    Save each decision and its reasons. Match baseline and challenger decisions on the same applications, then compare offers, dollars and modeled losses. The completed campaign also checks run coverage, saved settings and outcome consistency.

Original Module 2 architecture chartRouting order in SQLCounteroffer tests in SQLFinal outcomes in SQL

How to set parameters and run both programs in DBeaver

How many additional applicants receive an offer under the growth policy, and what do those offers do to total modeled loss? Use the two PostgreSQL programs in DBeaver and keep the applicants fixed while the lending rules change.

  1. Open a practice database. Connect DBeaver to a separate PostgreSQL database where your role can create tables and a schema. Open local copies of both SQL files. The scripts write to credit_decisioning_sim. Module 1 rebuilds its latest application table on each run. Its default SCENARIO_ONLY archive setting also replaces rows with the same scenario set, scenario name and population ID. Check the archive behavior.
  2. Build the applications once. In Module 1, find the Section 2 INSERT INTO tmp_module1_params. For this example, keep the shipped baseline values of MODULE1_V2_BASELINE_SET, BASELINE_V2, BASE_POPULATION_V1, 50,000 applications and archiving enabled. Select Sections 0–8.5 and use DBeaver’s Execute SQL Script in one session so the temporary tables stay available. Review Section 9’s product and score distributions, then confirm 50,000 archived rows in Section 10.1. Open the editable values · Module 1 parameter guide.
  3. Run the two policies. In Module 2, find the Section 2.1 INSERT INTO tmp_m2_operator_run_selector. Keep the active flag TRUE and run mode STANDARD_CAMPAIGN. Use the settings below for the first execution, then for the second. The run ID selects both the strategy and its product rules. The comparison ID identifies the two archived results to match. Open the selector · Module 2 parameter guide.
    Section 2.1 values for the baseline and growth runs
    Selector fieldFirst run · baselineSecond run · growth
    selected_module2_run_id'M2-01''M2-03'
    selected_comparison_group_id'CG02''CG02'
    section13_execution_mode'SKIP''REQUIRE'

    For each policy, execute Sections 1–2, inspect the resolved strategy and product settings in 2.11, and continue through Sections 3–16.8 in the same session. Commit each completed run if your connection uses manual commit. On the first pass, the challenger has yet to run. On the second, Section 13 can match both archived decisions for each application. Section 16.8 displays the saved run evidence. After all 39 campaign runs, rebuild Section 15, synchronize in 16.9, then run Section 17. Read the post-campaign sequence.

  4. Check the comparison. Look for 50,000 matched application IDs and zero differences in the checked source fields. In the saved CG02 results, 29,762 applicants received a baseline offer and 31,125 received a growth offer. The additional 1,363 net offers came with $238.42 million more offered and $8.68 million more modeled loss across the portfolio. Explore the original CG02 comparison.

    Product mix and credit-score mix

    Choose the fraction of applications in each category. Enter a decimal share from 0 to 1, for example 0.25 for 25%. The SQL checks each five-field total against 1 with an absolute tolerance of 0.000010. Keep every individual share within the probability range. Each mix uses its own repeatable draw, so realized counts can vary around the targets.

    Target shares · all fields are NUMERIC(12,6)
    Product shareBaselineScore-band shareBaseline
    pct_mortgage0.3 · 30%pct_super_prime0.18 · 18%
    pct_revolving0.25 · 25%pct_prime0.28 · 28%
    pct_auto0.2 · 20%pct_near_prime0.24 · 24%
    pct_personal_loan0.15 · 15%pct_subprime0.18 · 18%
    pct_heloc0.1 · 10%pct_deep_subprime0.12 · 12%

    The engine compares each draw with successive cumulative shares. Home equity lines and deep-subprime scores receive the final intervals. Moving five points of mix from prime to near-prime can change a borrower’s generated profile even when its application ID and draws stay fixed.

    revolving_base_min_payment_pctNUMERIC(12,6) · 0.020 to 0.10 inclusive. Base monthly share of the requested revolving line.
    revolving_interest_passthrough_factorNUMERIC(12,6) · 0.500 to 1 inclusive. Share of the monthly rate added to the base payment share. At zero, rate changes have no direct effect on this payment formula.

    Revolving monthly payment = requested line × [base payment share + (annual rate ÷ 12 × passthrough factor)]. For a $10,000 line at 24% APR, the baseline payment assumptions give $10,000 × (0.02 + 0.02 × 0.50) = $300 per month.

    Build the raw annual rate · Apply the product rate limits · Calculate the revolving payment

    Loss given default by product

    Loss given default (LGD) is the fraction of the balance the model assumes a lender loses if that borrower defaults. Enter a decimal strictly between 0 and 1. The same product-level assumption applies to every application of that product in the run.

    Loss severity · NUMERIC(12,6)
    ProductInputBaseline
    Mortgagelgd_mortgage0.2 · 20%
    Revolving credit linelgd_revolving0.85 · 85%
    Auto loanlgd_auto0.45 · 45%
    Unsecured personal loanlgd_personal0.7 · 70%
    Home equity linelgd_heloc0.25 · 25%

    Modeled loss on the request = requested amount × estimated default probability × LGD. Moving auto LGD from 0.45 to 0.55 raises loss on a $10,000 request at 8% estimated default probability from $360 to $440. Module 2 can then test whether an offer still meets its loss limit.

    Select two saved scenarios for the comparison report

    Module 2 · Set lending policy

    Module 2 applies a strategy and five product-specific policies to an existing Module 1 population. For a first comparison, keep the applications fixed and change the policy. The baseline and growth runs below can use exactly the same people, requested amounts, and loss assumptions.

    Select a run and a comparison

    In DBeaver, edit the values in the Section 2.1 INSERT in a working copy. The baseline row reads TRUE, 'STANDARD_CAMPAIGN', 'M2-01', NULL, 'AUTO'. To select the growth challenger for that same population, change the run ID to M2-03. Both archived runs feed comparison CG02. An explicit comparison selection changes the comparison report only.

    The values below are from BASELINE_STRATEGY_PROFILE. Percentages appear in reader units. Enter them in SQL as fractions, for example 0.08 for 8%. Modeled probability of default (PD) comes from Module 1. Module 2 uses these settings to act on that estimate.

    Review ceiling

    Each threshold is between 0 and 2. Approval < review ≤ decline.

    Set product limits and counteroffer rules

    Each product family supplies one row per product. The fields below show how to read those rows. The five-product baseline grid gives the exact starting values. A counteroffer enters sizing only after it clears the preliminary routing checks.

    Payment affordability
    SettingValues and use
    Approval PTI ceiling
    product_approve_max_pti    		Caps payment relative to income for a clean approval. 0 through 2. Target ≤ approval < review ≤ severe.
    Review PTI ceiling
    product_review_max_pti    		Used to classify the requested payment and detect borderline cases. The primary Section 6 PTI review trigger spans values above the approval ceiling and below the severe threshold. 0 through 2. Target ≤ approval < review ≤ severe.
    Severe PTI threshold
    product_decline_min_pti    		Flags severe payment burden on the original terms. 0 through 2. Target ≤ approval < review ≤ severe.
    Counteroffer target PTI
    counteroffer_target_pti    		Constrains the recalculated payment on a reduced offer. 0 through 2. Target ≤ approval < review ≤ severe.
    Expected loss in dollars
    SettingValues and use
    Approval loss ceiling
    product_approve_max_requested_el    		Requested expected-loss dollars at the clean-approval boundary. Nonnegative dollars. Approval < review ≤ severe.
    Review loss ceiling
    product_review_max_requested_el    		Diagnostic and borderline threshold for loss on the original request. The primary Section 6 loss review trigger spans values above the approval ceiling and below the severe threshold. Nonnegative dollars. Approval < review ≤ severe.
    Severe loss threshold
    product_decline_min_requested_el    		Severe original-terms expected-loss threshold. Nonnegative dollars. Approval < review ≤ severe.
    Counteroffer loss cap
    product_approved_el_cap    		Maximum modeled loss in dollars on a resized offer. For positive PD × loss given default (LGD), dividing this cap by PD × LGD gives a dollar ceiling on the offer. Nonnegative dollars. This cap is independent of the three requested-loss thresholds.
    Offer sizing
    SettingValues and use
    Minimum offer amount
    product_min_approved_amount    		Minimum product amount used to classify the request and test the size of a reduced offer. A positive dollar amount. Product minimum < product maximum.
    Maximum offer amount
    product_max_approved_amount    		Maximum exposure for the product and one ceiling used to size a reduced offer. A positive dollar amount. Product minimum < product maximum.
    Offer rounding increment
    approved_amount_rounding_increment    		Proposed counteroffers round down to this dollar increment before testing their floors. A positive dollar increment.
    Minimum share offered
    product_min_counteroffer_pct    		Minimum fraction of the original request that a reduced offer must retain. Fraction from 0 through 1.
    Maximum cut to exposure
    product_max_exposure_reduction_pct    		Maximum fraction that can be removed from the original request. The stricter of the two share-based floors applies. Fraction from 0 through 1.
    Resolution permissions
    SettingValues and use
    Allow counteroffers
    counteroffer_allowed_flag    		Enables the product for reduced-offer consideration; other eligibility and feasibility checks still apply. TRUE or FALSE.
    Allow manual review candidates
    manual_review_allowed_flag    		Permits the product to enter the explicit manual-review candidate rule. Failed structures and fallback routes have separate rules. TRUE or FALSE.

    For example, the baseline home equity line allows an offer as small as 40% of the request and allows a cut of up to 50%. On a $100,000 request, the minimum viable offer is the largest of $10,000 (product minimum), $40,000 (share floor), and $50,000 (maximum cut). The effective floor is $50,000. An offer must still fit the applicable upper bounds and rounding rule.

    exposure_assignment_method    		Uses the most conservative feasible offer amount. Allowed values · MOST_CONSERVATIVE_FEASIBLE_AMOUNT. Baseline · MOST_CONSERVATIVE_FEASIBLE_AMOUNT.

    Verify the fixed outcome conventions · Inspect the archive key and replacement scope

    Read the derived counteroffer variant and switches

    Section 2.6C derives the variant from the strategy name. The aggressive profile enables all six switches together and can test some requests with severe payment, exposure or requested-loss signals. A hard policy stop, severe modeled default risk, or severe DTI still takes priority. A candidate must pass the same size and economic feasibility checks.

    Values generated from the selected profile
    SettingValues and use
    Counteroffer strategy variant
    counteroffer_strategy_variant    		The baseline and other ordinary strategies use NOT_COUNTEROFFER_SPLIT_STRATEGY. The selective profile and its legacy alias use SELECTIVE_FEASIBILITY. The aggressive profile uses AGGRESSIVE_EXPANSION.
    Aggressive expansion
    aggressive_counteroffer_expansion_enabled    		Derived Boolean. TRUE for aggressive expansion and FALSE for the other strategy names.
    Severe requested terms
    severe_requested_structure_counteroffer_override_enabled    		Derived Boolean. TRUE for aggressive expansion and FALSE for the other strategy names.
    Extreme exposure

    Module 1 release validation in Power BI

    The teaching explorer above compares credit policies. This downloadable workbook follows the same 50,000 baseline applications through Module 1 v1.0 and v2.0. Start with Executive Summary to see the scale of the change. In Release Impact Explorer, select an application to see which values changed and by how much.

    At least one of seven fields changed for 21,326 applicants. The dashboard keeps the other 28,674 in view so you can see the full comparison.
